html:
German builds words a lot like Chinese does: you can simply string nouns together to make new ones. Because the original words stay intact, it’s much easier to work out what a new word means.

Take the pantograph on top of a train. In German it’s a Stromaufnehmer: Strom means electricity, and aufnehmer comes from the root aufnehmen, roughly English “take,” in the sense of picking something up. The n turning into r works much as in English, making a noun out of a verb. Just as with the Chinese word for it, literally a “current-receiving bow,” you can tell what the thing does even if you’ve never seen the word before. And English? Pantograph. Good luck figuring out what that is.

Lunch is Mittagessen. Mittag means noon and Essen means meal, exactly like the Chinese “noon meal,” and much more transparent than lunch.

Directivity: Richt (pointing) + charakteristik (-ity), mirroring the Chinese term piece by piece.

Polyhedra are an absolute disaster in English. A twelve-faced solid is a dodecahedron in English, but in German it’s a Zwölfflächner, a “twelve-facer.” German does have a word that matches the English one, but I suspect that’s an import from English.
